docs.title: NUOX: constrained learning with JAX and Optax
docs.text:
Define a loss. Define a constraint. Train with NUOX.

NUOX provides an Optax transformation for differentiable equality-constrained optimisation:

\[ \min_\theta \mathcal L(\theta) \quad\text{subject to}\quad c(\theta)=0. \]

The constraint function returns residuals: zero means the specified conditions are satisfied. NUOX projects a proposed direction onto the null space of the constraint Jacobian and adds a correction for existing violations. LSMR computes the required least-squares solution using Jacobian products, without constructing the full Jacobian.

Start with the runnable quick-start, then read about constraints and optimizer composition. The tutorials apply the same workflow to PINNs, one-step generation, and LLM editing. The API reference describes the current interfaces.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
From a checkout containing pyproject.toml:

git clone https://github.com/h-roy/nuox.git
cd nuox
python -m pip install -e .

Use the official JAX installation guide to configure GPU support. The core quick-start also runs on CPU. Tutorial-specific dependencies belong to each notebook's setup.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Constraints must be differentiable with respect to the optimized parameters. Enforcement is numerical and local: nonlinear residuals depend on the step size, solver accuracy, and feasibility. A constraint evaluated at selected inputs protects those inputs; it does not establish a global property of the model.

The bundled LSMR solver operates on one-dimensional arrays. Flatten parameter PyTrees and return a flat residual vector, as shown in the guide. Core training does not require differentiating through the optimizer or wrapping its least-squares solver in a custom derivative.

Source code · Issues · MIT license

docs.title: Projection transform
docs.text: make_project_grad returns an Optax transformation. Initialize it with the optimized parameter vector and call update(direction, state, (params, args, kwargs)). The constraint is evaluated as constraint_fn(params, *args, **kwargs).

docs.title: nuox.optax_nullspace.make_project_grad(constraint_fn, *, wm_epochs, num_batches, gamma, least_squares_solver, scale_gamma=False)
docs.text:
Create a null-space projection transform for Optax.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default constraint_fn ConstraintFn

Callable returning the constraint violation for a given set of parameters. Signature: constraint_fn(params, *model_args, **kwargs).

required wm_epochs int

Warmup epochs where the projection is skipped.

required num_batches int

Number of batches per epoch used to compute warmup steps.

required gamma float

Rate used for the Gauss-Newton correction term.

required least_squares_solver LeastSquaresSolver

Callable implementing the least-squares solve. Must accept (vecmat, rhs, vecmat_args=()) and return (solution, stats).

required scale_gamma bool

If True, scale gamma by the constraint norm.

False Source code in nuox/optax_nullspace.py 
def make_project_grad(
    constraint_fn: ConstraintFn,
    *,
    wm_epochs: int,
    num_batches: int,
    gamma: float,
    least_squares_solver: LeastSquaresSolver,
    scale_gamma: bool = False,
) -> optax.GradientTransformation:
    """Create a null-space projection transform for Optax.

    Args:
        constraint_fn: Callable returning the constraint violation for a given set
            of parameters. Signature: ``constraint_fn(params, *model_args, **kwargs)``.
        wm_epochs: Warmup epochs where the projection is skipped.
        num_batches: Number of batches per epoch used to compute warmup steps.
        gamma: Rate used for the Gauss-Newton correction term.
        least_squares_solver: Callable implementing the least-squares solve.
            Must accept ``(vecmat, rhs, vecmat_args=())`` and return
            ``(solution, stats)``.
        scale_gamma: If ``True``, scale ``gamma`` by the constraint norm.
    """

    ops_builder = build_constraint_ops(constraint_fn)

    def lstsq_grad(grads, params, *model_args, **constraint_kwargs):
        matvec, vecmat = ops_builder(*model_args, **constraint_kwargs)
        constraint = constraint_fn(params, *model_args, **constraint_kwargs)

        if scale_gamma:
            scaled_gamma = gamma * jnp.linalg.norm(constraint)
        else:
            scaled_gamma = gamma

        rhs = matvec(grads, params) - scaled_gamma * constraint
        lstsq_grads, _ = least_squares_solver(vecmat, rhs, vecmat_args=(params,))
        return grads - lstsq_grads

    def init_fn(_params):
        return ProjState(count=jnp.zeros([], dtype=jnp.int32))

    def update_fn(updates, state, update_params):
        params, model_args, constraint_kwargs = update_params
        num_steps = state.count
        project = lambda u: lstsq_grad(u, params, *model_args, **constraint_kwargs)
        updates = jax.lax.cond(
            num_steps > wm_epochs * num_batches,
            project,
            lambda u: u,
            updates,
        )
        next_state = ProjState(count=num_steps + 1)
        return updates, next_state

    return optax.GradientTransformation(init_fn, update_fn)

Jacobian products
docs.text: build_constraint_ops(constraint_fn)(*args, **kwargs) returns (matvec, vecmat). Their signatures are matvec(v, params) for \(Jv\) and vecmat(w, params) for \(J^T w\).

docs.title: nuox.operators.build_constraint_ops(constraint_fn)
docs.text:
Return matvec and rmatvec closures for the constraint Jacobian.

The returned callable expects positional model_args and keyword constraint arguments. When invoked with concrete values, it produces two functions:

matvec(v, params) applies the Jacobian of constraint_fn to v. vecmat(v, params) applies the transpose Jacobian to v.

Source code in nuox/operators.py 
def build_constraint_ops(constraint_fn: ConstraintFn) -> Callable[..., LinearOp]:
    """Return matvec and rmatvec closures for the constraint Jacobian.

    The returned callable expects positional ``model_args`` and keyword constraint
    arguments. When invoked with concrete values, it produces two functions:

    ``matvec(v, params)`` applies the Jacobian of ``constraint_fn`` to ``v``.
    ``vecmat(v, params)`` applies the transpose Jacobian to ``v``.
    """

    def make_ops(*model_args, **constraint_kwargs):
        def constrained_params_fn(p):
            return constraint_fn(p, *model_args, **constraint_kwargs)

        def matvec(v, params):
            return jax.jvp(constrained_params_fn, (params,), (v,))[1]

        def vecmat(v, params):
            _, vjp_fn = jax.vjp(constrained_params_fn, params)
            return vjp_fn(v)[0]

        return matvec, vecmat

    return make_ops

docs.title: LSMR
docs.text: The factory returns a callable with signature solver(vecmat, rhs, vecmat_args=()). Here vecmat(w, *vecmat_args) must compute \(A^T w\); the solver returns a solution to the least-squares problem \(Ax \approx \mathrm{rhs}\) and a statistics dictionary. Inputs and outputs are one-dimensional arrays. The guide explains tolerances and iteration budgets.

docs.title: nuox.linalg.lstsq_lsmr(*, atol=1e-06, btol=1e-06, ctol=1e-08, maxiter=1000000, damp=0.0, while_loop=jax.lax.while_loop)
docs.text:
LSMR -- like in SciPy, but using JAX.

Source code in nuox/linalg.py 
def lstsq_lsmr(
    *,
    atol: float = 1e-6,
    btol: float = 1e-6,
    ctol: float = 1e-8,
    maxiter: int = 1_000_000,
    damp=0.0,
    while_loop=jax.lax.while_loop,
) -> Solver:
    """LSMR -- like in SciPy, but using JAX."""

    @register_dataclass
    @dataclasses.dataclass
    class State:
        itn: int
        alpha: float
        u: jax.Array
        v: jax.Array
        alphabar: float
        rhobar: float
        rho: float
        zeta: float
        sbar: float
        cbar: float
        zetabar: float
        hbar: jax.Array
        h: jax.Array
        x: jax.Array
        betadd: float
        thetatilde: float
        rhodold: float
        betad: float
        tautildeold: float
        d: float
        normA2: float
        maxrbar: float
        minrbar: float
        normA: float
        condA: float
        normx: float
        normar: float
        normr: float
        istop: int

    def run(vecmat, b, vecmat_args=()):
        def vecmat_noargs(v):
            return vecmat(v, *vecmat_args)

        (ncols,) = jax.eval_shape(vecmat, b, *vecmat_args).shape
        state, normb, matvec_noargs = init(vecmat_noargs, b, ncols=ncols)
        step_fun = make_step(matvec_noargs, normb=normb)
        cond_fun = make_cond_fun()
        state = while_loop(cond_fun, step_fun, state)
        stats_ = stats(state)
        return state.x, stats_

    def init(vecmat, b, ncols: int):
        normb = jnp.linalg.norm(b)
        x = jnp.zeros(ncols, b.dtype)
        beta = normb

        u = b / jnp.where(beta > 0, beta, 1.0)

        v, matvec = jax.vjp(vecmat, u)
        alpha = jnp.linalg.norm(v)
        v = v / jnp.where(alpha > 0, alpha, 1)
        v = jnp.where(beta == 0, jnp.zeros_like(v), v)
        alpha = jnp.where(beta == 0, jnp.zeros_like(alpha), alpha)

        zetabar = alpha * beta
        alphabar = alpha
        rho = 1.0
        rhobar = 1.0
        cbar = 1.0
        sbar = 0.0

        h = v
        hbar = jnp.zeros(ncols, b.dtype)

        betadd = beta
        betad = 0.0
        rhodold = 1.0
        tautildeold = 0.0
        thetatilde = 0.0
        zeta = 0.0
        d = 0.0

        normA2 = alpha * alpha
        maxrbar = 0.0
        minrbar = 1e10
        normA = jnp.sqrt(normA2)
        condA = 1.0
        normx = 0.0

        normr = beta
        normar = alpha * beta

        state = State(
            itn=0,
            alpha=alpha,
            u=u,
            v=v,
            alphabar=alphabar,
            rho=rho,
            rhobar=rhobar,
            zeta=zeta,
            sbar=sbar,
            cbar=cbar,
            zetabar=zetabar,
            hbar=hbar,
            h=h,
            x=x,
            betadd=betadd,
            thetatilde=thetatilde,
            rhodold=rhodold,
            betad=betad,
            tautildeold=tautildeold,
            d=d,
            normA2=normA2,
            maxrbar=maxrbar,
            minrbar=minrbar,
            normar=normar,
            normr=normr,
            normA=normA,
            condA=condA,
            normx=normx,
            # x=0 is already the minimum-norm solution if b=0 or A.T @ b=0.
            # A bidiagonalization step would divide by zero in either exact case.
            istop=jnp.where(beta == 0, 8, jnp.where(alpha == 0, 9, 0)),
        )
        state = jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda z: jnp.asarray(z), state)
        return state, normb, lambda *a: matvec(*a)[0]

    def make_step(matvec, normb: float) -> Callable:
        def step(state: State) -> State:
            Av, A_t = jax.vjp(matvec, state.v)
            u = Av - state.alpha * state.u
            beta = jnp.linalg.norm(u)

            u = u / jnp.where(beta > 0, beta, 1.0)
            v = A_t(u)[0] - beta * state.v
            alpha = jnp.linalg.norm(v)
            v = v / jnp.where(alpha > 0, alpha, 1)

            chat, shat, alphahat = _sym_ortho(state.alphabar, damp)

            rhoold = state.rho
            c, s, rho = _sym_ortho(alphahat, beta)
            thetanew = s * alpha
            alphabar = c * alpha

            rhobarold = state.rhobar
            zetaold = state.zeta
            thetabar = state.sbar * rho
            rhotemp = state.cbar * rho
            cbar, sbar, rhobar = _sym_ortho(rhotemp, thetanew)
            zeta = cbar * state.zetabar
            zetabar = -sbar * state.zetabar

            hbar = state.h - state.hbar * (thetabar * rho / (rhoold * rhobarold))
            x = state.x + (zeta / (rho * rhobar)) * hbar
            h = v - state.h * (thetanew / rho)

            betaacute = chat * state.betadd
            betacheck = -shat * state.betadd

            betahat = c * betaacute
            betadd = -s * betaacute

            thetatildeold = state.thetatilde
            ctildeold, stildeold, rhotildeold = _sym_ortho(state.rhodold, thetabar)
            thetatilde = stildeold * rhobar
            rhodold = ctildeold * rhobar
            betad = -stildeold * state.betad + ctildeold * betahat

            tautildeold = (zetaold - thetatildeold * state.tautildeold) / rhotildeold
            taud = (zeta - thetatilde * tautildeold) / rhodold
            d = state.d + betacheck * betacheck
            normr = jnp.sqrt(d + (betad - taud) ** 2 + betadd * betadd)

            normA2 = state.normA2 + beta * beta
            normA = jnp.sqrt(normA2)
            normA2 = normA2 + alpha * alpha

            maxrbar = jnp.maximum(state.maxrbar, rhobarold)
            minrbar = jnp.where(state.itn > 1, jnp.minimum(state.minrbar, rhobarold), state.minrbar)
            condA = jnp.maximum(maxrbar, rhotemp) / jnp.minimum(minrbar, rhotemp)

            normar = jnp.abs(zetabar)
            normx = jnp.linalg.norm(x)

            itn = state.itn + 1
            test1 = normr / normb
            z = normA * normr
            z_safe = jnp.where(z != 0, z, 1.0)
            test2 = jnp.where(z != 0, normar / z_safe, LARGE_VALUE)
            test3 = 1 / condA
            t1 = test1 / (1 + normA * normx / normb)
            rtol = btol + atol * normA * normx / normb

            istop = 0
            istop = jnp.where(normar == 0, 9, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(normb == 0, 8, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(itn >= maxiter, 7, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(1 + test3 <= 1, 6, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(1 + test2 <= 1, 5, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(1 + t1 <= 1, 4, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(test3 <= ctol, 3, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(test2 <= atol, 2, istop)
            istop = jnp.where(test1 <= rtol, 1, istop)

            return State(
                itn=itn,
                alpha=alpha,
                u=u,
                v=v,
                alphabar=alphabar,
                rho=rho,
                rhobar=rhobar,
                zeta=zeta,
                sbar=sbar,
                cbar=cbar,
                zetabar=zetabar,
                hbar=hbar,
                h=h,
                x=x,
                betadd=betadd,
                thetatilde=thetatilde,
                rhodold=rhodold,
                betad=betad,
                tautildeold=tautildeold,
                d=d,
                normA2=normA2,
                maxrbar=maxrbar,
                minrbar=minrbar,
                normar=normar,
                normr=normr,
                normA=normA,
                condA=condA,
                normx=normx,
                istop=istop,
            )

        return step

    def make_cond_fun() -> Callable:
        def cond(state):
            state_flat, _ = jax.flatten_util.ravel_pytree(state)
            no_nans = jnp.logical_not(jnp.any(jnp.isnan(state_flat)))
            proceed = jnp.where(state.istop == 0, True, False)
            return jnp.logical_and(proceed, no_nans)

        return cond

    def stats(state: State) -> dict:
        return {
            "iteration_count": state.itn,
            "norm_residual": state.normr,
            "norm_At_residual": state.normar,
            "norm_A": state.normA,
            "cond_A": state.condA,
            "norm_x": state.normx,
            "istop": state.istop,
        }

    return run

Legacy training helper
docs.text: make_update_fn(loss_fn, optim, constr_fn) returns a jitted function accepting (params, opt_state, x, y, **constr_params). It returns (loss_before_update, new_params, new_opt_state, constraint_after_update). New examples use an explicit training step to make the constraint arguments visible.

docs.title: nuox.optax_nullspace.make_update_fn(loss_fn, optim, constr_fn)
docs.text:
Create an Optax-compatible update function matching the legacy API.

Source code in nuox/optax_nullspace.py 
def make_update_fn(loss_fn, optim, constr_fn):
    """Create an Optax-compatible update function matching the legacy API."""

    @jax.jit
    def update_fn(params, opt_state, x, y, **constr_params):
        loss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn)(params, x, y)
        updates, opt_state = optim.update(grads, opt_state, (params, (), constr_params))
        params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)
        constraint_value = constr_fn(params, **constr_params)
        return loss, params, opt_state, constraint_value

    return update_fn

docs.title: Return a vector of residuals
docs.text:
For a condition \(f_\theta(x)=y\), return f(params, x) - y. For a scalar condition, use jnp.atleast_1d. For multiple outputs, flatten and concatenate the residuals:

# Fragment: predict is your model's forward function.
def constraint_fn(params, inputs, *, targets):
    return (predict(params, inputs) - targets).reshape(-1)

# Inside a training step:
updates, state = optimizer.update(
    grads, state, (params, (inputs,), {"targets": targets})
)

Keep array shapes fixed across compiled steps. Pass changing batches through the argument tuple rather than mutating captured Python state. Keep differentiable computations in JAX.

Do not replace a vector residual by its squared norm just to reduce the number of constraints: the derivative of that scalar vanishes at feasibility, changing the projection problem. Scale residual components deliberately when their units or magnitudes differ. Unequal scaling affects numerical conditioning and, for inconsistent systems, the least-squares compromise.

docs.title: Flatten model parameters
docs.text:
The bundled LSMR implementation expects a one-dimensional parameter array and a one-dimensional residual array. Use ravel_pytree for a model with nested parameters:

from jax.flatten_util import ravel_pytree

# Fragment: initial_params, model_loss and model_constraint are your model's API.
params, unravel = ravel_pytree(initial_params)

def loss_fn(flat_params, batch):
    return model_loss(unravel(flat_params), batch)

def constraint_fn(flat_params, inputs):
    return model_constraint(unravel(flat_params), inputs).reshape(-1)

The optimized vector can be converted back with unravel(params). For Flax Linen, vectorize_model provides a forward function that accepts this vector:

from nuox import vectorize_model

# Fragment: model is an initialized Linen module and variables its collections.
apply_vec, params, unravel = vectorize_model(
    model, params=variables["params"], variables=variables
)
# Predictions: apply_vec(params, inputs)

The helper is for a functional forward pass. It does not persist changed mutable collections; manage state such as running statistics explicitly when training a stateful model.

docs.title: Compose the optimizer
docs.text:
The simplest composition is constrained SGD:

optimizer = optax.chain(projection, optax.scale(-lr))

If using Adam's adaptive direction, apply it before projection:

optimizer = optax.chain(
    optax.scale_by_adam(),
    projection,
    optax.scale(-lr),
)

This preserves the linearized constraint relation of the projected direction, up to solve error. It does not guarantee convergence to the same constrained optimum as projected SGD. Coordinate-wise scaling, momentum, or weight decay applied after projection can invalidate that relation. The params argument received by every chained transform is NUOX's (params, args, kwargs) tuple, so transforms that expect an ordinary parameter tree need a suitable adapter.

docs.title: Correction strength and warmup
docs.text:
Write \(J\) for the constraint Jacobian and \(g\) for the direction entering NUOX. With an exact, undamped, minimum-norm solve, the transform returns

\[ \widetilde g = g-J^+(Jg-\gamma c), \qquad \Delta\theta=-\eta\widetilde g. \]

If the linearized correction is feasible, \(J\Delta\theta=-\eta\gamma c\). For an affine constraint this reduces the residual by a factor \(1-\eta\gamma\). For nonlinear constraints this is a first-order relation. A rank-deficient or inconsistent system may leave an uncorrectable residual.

The quick-start sets gamma=0.2 / lr, correcting 20% of the linearized violation per step. gamma=0 only projects the direction and does not repair an existing violation. With a learning-rate schedule and fixed gamma, the correction fraction changes with the learning rate. scale_gamma=True additionally multiplies gamma by the current residual norm; leave it off for the simple fixed-fraction interpretation.

Projection runs when state.count > wm_epochs * num_batches, with the count initialized to zero. Thus wm_epochs=-1, num_batches=1 starts immediately, while wm_epochs=0 leaves the first update unconstrained. These arguments control a step-count threshold; NUOX does not manage epochs or batching.

docs.title: Choose a least-squares solver
docs.text:
Start with an explicit iteration budget:

from nuox.linalg import lstsq_lsmr

solver = lstsq_lsmr(atol=1e-6, btol=1e-6, maxiter=64)

64 is a starting budget, not a universal convergence guarantee. Increase it if the linear solve is too inaccurate. atol and btol govern residual stopping criteria; ctol is a reciprocal condition-estimate threshold. damp regularizes the solve and changes the projection/correction. The current default maxiter is one million, so set a finite budget appropriate to your problem.

lstsq_jnp() materializes the Jacobian and is useful for small debugging problems. Normal-equation solvers are also available, but forming normal equations can worsen conditioning. Dense solvers are unsuitable for large parameter Jacobians.

The projection transform currently discards solver statistics. Direct solver calls return (solution, stats), with LSMR statistics including iteration_count, norm_residual, norm_At_residual, and istop.

docs.title: Monitor what matters
docs.text:
Track the task loss and the residual after applying each update:

residual = constraint_fn(params, inputs, targets=targets)
rms = jnp.sqrt(jnp.mean(residual**2))
maximum = jnp.max(jnp.abs(residual))

If residuals increase, check the optimizer order and warmup first. Then inspect solver accuracy, reduce the learning rate or correction fraction, and check whether the requested conditions are mutually compatible. Separately evaluate held-out inputs when the intended property should generalize beyond the constraint points.

docs.title: Quick-start
docs.text:
Fit three parameters to [1, 2, 3] while requiring their sum to equal one. This is a complete CPU-compatible example; paste it into a notebook cell or run python tutorials/minimal.py from the repository root after installing dependencies.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax

from nuox import make_project_grad
from nuox.linalg import lstsq_lsmr


# 1. Define the loss and constraint residual.
def loss_fn(params):
    return jnp.mean((params - jnp.array([1., 2., 3.])) ** 2)


def constraint_fn(params):
    return jnp.atleast_1d(params.sum() - 1.)


# 2. Create a constrained SGD optimizer.
lr = 0.05
projection = make_project_grad(
    constraint_fn,
    wm_epochs=-1,  # Activate from the first update.
    num_batches=1,
    gamma=0.2 / lr,  # Correct 20% of the linearized violation per step.
    least_squares_solver=lstsq_lsmr(maxiter=32),
)
optimizer = optax.chain(projection, optax.scale(-lr))


# 3. Train with the usual JAX/Optax loop.
@jax.jit
def step(params, state):
    grads = jax.grad(loss_fn)(params)
    updates, state = optimizer.update(grads, state, (params, (), {}))
    return optax.apply_updates(params, updates), state


params = jnp.zeros(3)
state = optimizer.init(params)

for _ in range(500):
    params, state = step(params, state)

print("Parameters:", params)
print("Constraint error:", float(jnp.linalg.norm(constraint_fn(params))))

The solution should be close to [-0.6667, 0.3333, 1.3333], with constraint error below 1e-5 in this example. This checks both feasibility and the correct constrained optimum.

constraint_fn returns a residual, not a penalty loss. make_project_grad defines the constrained direction; optax.scale(-lr) turns it into a parameter update. The extra tuple passed to update supplies parameters and arguments for evaluating the constraint.

wm_epochs=-1 activates projection on the first update. With the current implementation, wm_epochs=0 skips the first update. See the guide for the correction strength and warmup semantics.

docs.title: Quick checks and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Run these from the repository root, which contains pyproject.toml:

python -m pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"
python -c "import nuox; from nuox import make_project_grad; print(nuox.__file__)"
python tutorials/minimal.py
python tutorials/vectorize_model_demo.py
python -m pytest -q
python -m mkdocs build --strict

The import should point to the inner nuox/__init__.py. The minimal example should reach approximately [-0.6667, 0.3333, 1.3333] with constraint error below 1e-5. Tests must pass, and the strict documentation build must exit successfully. These checks do not require the large tutorials or model downloads.

To also execute the exact code printed in the quick-start, run:

python scripts/check_quickstart.py

To preview the site:

python -m mkdocs serve

Open the URL printed by MkDocs, normally http://127.0.0.1:8000. Check that equations render and navigation works. If running on a remote machine, forward port 8000 through your editor or SSH connection. A successful build checks local documentation links, but does not verify external websites or whether tutorial notebooks have been pushed to GitHub.

docs.title: ImportError: cannot import name 'make_project_grad'
docs.text:
If the error says unknown location, Python may have found the outer repository folder as a namespace rather than the installed package. Install with the same interpreter used to run the example:

python -m pip install -e .
python -c "import sys, nuox; print(sys.executable); print(nuox.__file__)"

Run the installation from the directory containing pyproject.toml, not its parent. In a notebook, use %pip install -e /absolute/path/to/nuox for your checkout, then restart the kernel. A cached namespace import can survive an installation until the kernel restarts. Avoid naming a local script nuox.py.

docs.title: GPU not visible
docs.text: Check jax.devices() in the process that actually runs training. On a cluster, that process or notebook kernel must run inside a GPU allocation. An allocated GPU shell does not move a kernel already running on a login node. Use the JAX installation guide linked on the home page for the appropriate GPU build.

docs.title: Constraints are not being enforced
docs.text: Check that projection has started (wm_epochs=-1 starts immediately), the constraint returns residuals rather than a squared penalty, and no coordinate-wise transform follows projection. Inspect solver accuracy and the learning-rate/correction settings in the guide.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each notebook follows task → loss → constraint → NUOX optimizer → training → visualization. These examples demonstrate different uses of the same interface.

Notebook Objective Constraint What to inspect PINNs Minimize a differential-equation residual Initial conditions at selected points Solution heatmaps and initial-condition errors. One-step flow matching Distil a flow model into a fast generator Preserve selected instantaneous teacher velocities Ordinary FM and NUOX samples at one, two, and four steps. LLM editing Fit an edited fact Restrict changes to an editable weight matrix Original and edited answers, including held-out prompts.

docs.title: Run a notebook
docs.text:
Keep the notebook, its Python helpers, and data files together. In VS Code, select the intended Python kernel, restart it, and run from the setup cell. In Colab, follow the setup cell and upload the tutorial bundle if prompted. A GPU runtime must be selected before initializing JAX to use a GPU.

The notebooks include setup for CPU and GPU. Runtime depends on the model, hardware, compilation, and first-time downloads. Check the notebook's actual device before attributing a timing to GPU execution.

docs.title: Interpret the examples
docs.text:
For PINNs, satisfying sampled initial conditions does not by itself guarantee an accurate solution throughout the domain. For flow distillation, assess generation quality alongside velocity-constraint residuals; the student also receives distillation supervision. For LLM editing, preserving selected weight-space directions does not guarantee unchanged answers or correct logical consequences everywhere.

The notebooks contain the experiment settings and visual comparisons. They are demonstrations of constrained learning, not a claim of universal improvement over unconstrained methods.
